d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_benefits:
Improved tumor control, assessed by reduction in tumor size (RECIST Nano) and clinical symptoms, compared to radiation therapy alone

Enhanced quality of life, evaluated using a standardized assessment grid completed by the owner before, during, and after treatment

Increased longevity, measured by overall survival

Potential for complete response in a subset of patients
d_avma_studycontent_data.potential_risks: Risks include those associated with anesthesia required for MRI and radiation delivery, as well as risks related to the nanoparticle injection, such as anaphylactic reaction,
d_avma_studycontent_data.inclusion_criteria:
Dogs with glioma tumors confirmed by biopsy, surgery, or suspected based on MRI findings (as reviewed by a board-certified radiologist or neurologist) are eligible for enrollment.

Both primary tumors and recurrences following surgery may be included.

Patients currently receiving chemotherapy (e.g., temozolomide or lomustine) must discontinue treatment and undergo a washout period of at least two weeks prior to enrollment.

Steroid and anticonvulsant therapies may be continued as prescribed.

All antioxidant supplements, including those marketed as aging or cognitive support medications, must be discontinued. Please consult your primary veterinarian or our study team with any questions or concerns regarding medications or supplements.
d_avma_studycontent_data.exclusion_criteria:
Dogs with a history of prior tumor irradiation

Dogs currently undergoing chemotherapy

Dogs receiving other forms of immunotherapy

These patients are not eligible for enrollment in the study.
d_avma_studycontent_data.intervention_name:
Prior to treatment, the patient will undergo a CT scan and a repeat MRI if deemed necessary. All imaging will be performed under short-duration anesthesia and will be used to develop the radiation treatment plan.

Radiation therapy will consist of stereotactic treatment with 8 Gy delivered on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, for a total dose of 24 Gy. Each treatment session will require short-duration anesthesia. Radiation will be delivered using an Elekta Evo linear accelerator equipped for stereotactic treatments.

The nanoparticle will be administered once prior to the initiation of radiation therapy, followed by additional doses during the treatment week on Tuesday and Thursday, and once more on the Wednesday following the completion of radiation.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_measure: Adverse events will be documented based on VCO immunotherapy criteria and using a standardized grid anesthesia-related adverse effects and radiation-associated toxicities as defined by VRTOG (Veterinary Radiation Therapy Oncology Group) grades I and II.
d_avma_studycontent_data.pri_outcome_endpoint:
Censoring Guidelines:

Participants will be censored under the following conditions:

  1. Protocol non-compliance: Patients who do not adhere to the prescribed treatment schedule (e.g., missed radiation sessions or investigational drug injections) without a justified reason.
  2. Loss to follow-up: Patients who are unreachable for scheduled evaluations
  3. Unrelated mortality: Deaths clearly attributable to causes unrelated to the disease under investigation (e.g., trauma, cardiac arrest without oncologic link) will be considered as events but not disease-related endpoints.

Study Stopping Criteria:

The study will be halted, either temporarily or permanently, if:

  1. A serious adverse event (SAE) occurs that is determined to be likely related to the intervention (e.g., CAR-modified cell injection or radiation), and is not responsive to standard of care management.
  2. A pre-specified threshold of SAEs or treatment-related deaths is met, as defined in the Data and Safety Monitoring Plan (DSMP).
  3. The Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) recommends early termination due to unacceptable toxicity
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_measure: MRI and clinical recheck data will be collected, along with regular phone follow-ups.
d_avma_studycontent_data.sec_outcome1_endpoint:
PFS curve and Kaplan Meier curves

Censorship

Loss to follow-up: Patients who are unreachable for scheduled evaluations despite documented efforts.

Unrelated mortality: Deaths clearly attributable to causes unrelated to the disease under investigation (e.g., trauma, cardiac arrest without oncologic link) will be considered as events but not disease-related endpoints.

d_sv_content.name: Treating Dogs With Glioma Using Radiation and Immunotherapy
d_sv_content.description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that pose significant therapeutic challenges in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by locally invasive growth and poor overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds—particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers—are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy may also be used as a standalone treatment, delivered through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT). SRT offers the advantages of high precision, greater tissue sparing, and shorter treatment duration. Despite these interventions, the prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. Their natural disease course, intact immune system, and clinically comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable for evaluating the efficacy and safety of emerging therapies.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy. In this study, we investigate the combination of stereotactic radiation therapy with an FDA-approved nanoparticle, previously shown to be safe in dogs. This nanoparticle has demonstrated the ability in rodent models to modulate the tumor immune microenvironment by transforming tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from an M2 (pro-tumor) to an M1 (anti-tumor) phenotype.
